name: Tese
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: The These language has three level tones and two contour tones. The level tones are High, Mid and Low. The contour tones are rising and falling. Low tone and High tone are the most common ones, while Mid tone is less common. The falling tone only occurs at the last syllable, and rising tone is rare in my data. More study is needed for tones. [...] Tone is distinctive at the lexical level. [...] Tone also distinguishes the verb aspect.
new_statements.citation: Yip, May. 2004. Phonology of the These language. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 93-117. Entebbe: SIL-Sudan.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 3 'Tone', printed p. 108 (PDF p. 114 of; p. 16 of the extracted article PDF)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quoted passage is verbatim at sec. 3 'Tone', printed p. 108 = volume PDF p. 114: "The These language has three level tones and two contour tones. The level tones are High, Mid and Low. The contour tones are rising and falling. Low tone and High tone are the most common ones, while Mid tone is less common. The falling tone only occurs at the last syllable, and rising tone is rare in my data. More study is needed for tones." then "Tone is distinctive at the lexical level." and "Tone also distinguishes the verb aspect." Minor locator slip only: the extracted article PDF has its pages ordered printed 94-117 with printed 93 as the last page, so printed p. 108 is its p. 15, not p. 16. grep of…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tese is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus falling and rising contours; tone is lexically contrastive and marks verb aspect (with consonant gemination). The article, the only phonological description of the language, contains no statement about word stress or accent at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Falling tone restricted to the final syllable; rising tone rare; mid tone less common and left unmarked in the orthography.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone and verb-aspect tone; citation-form data from Khartoum-based speakers. Silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Yip's 'These' = Tesei Umm Danab = Glottolog tese1238 (dialect teis1234). Glottolog folds 'Keiga Jirru' (keig1243) into tese1238 as a dialect and lists it as an alternative name, following Ethnologue; Blench 2013 and Stevenson's notes treat Keiga Jirru (autonym Doni) as a distinct third Temein language, and Yip herself says the These people regard These and Keiga Jirru as one language in different dialects. Not to be confused with Keiga (Kadu family, keig1242).

sources.note: Full phonology (consonants incl. gemination, 10-vowel ATR system, vowel length, sec. 3 Tone, sec. 4 morphology). The word 'stress' occurs nowhere in the article; no accent/prominence statement.
